(p-455) Surat Hud (p-455) is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night﴾ [Hud: 114].

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm, then detailed, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ ﴿that you worship none but Allah. Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term and will give every doer of virtue his virtue. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ ﴿To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent﴾

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book﴾ means the Qur'an.

﴿whose verses have been made firm, then detailed﴾ has five interpretations. The first: its verses were made firm by command and prohibition, then detailed by reward and punishment; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: its verses were made firm from falsehood, then detailed with the lawful and unlawful, obedience and disobedience; this is the view of Qatadah.

(p-456) The third: its verses were made firm in that all the verses of this surah were made firm, then detailed in that they were explained; this is the meaning of Mujahid's view.

The fourth: its verses were made firm for those who take heed, and its verses were detailed for those who are God-fearing.

The fifth: its verses were made firm in the hearts, and its rulings were detailed upon the bodies.

﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ has two meanings. One: from One who is wise in His actions, aware of the welfare of His servants.

The second: wise in what He sent down, aware of who will accept it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾ has two meanings. One: that it is written in the Book, "that you worship none but Allah." The second: that He commanded His Messenger to say to the people, "that you worship none but Allah," ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a warner from the Fire, and a bringer of good tidings of Paradise.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾ has two meanings. One: seek His forgiveness for your past sins, then turn to Him in repentance from what you commit anew whenever it occurs from you.

Some scholars said: seeking forgiveness without ceasing from sin is the repentance of liars.

The second: He mentioned seeking forgiveness first because forgiveness is the sought goal, and repentance is the means to it; so forgiveness is first in the seeking and last in the cause.

It may also bear a third meaning: seek His forgiveness for minor sins, and turn to Him in repentance from major sins. ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾, meaning in this world, and it has three aspects. One: it is contentment of soul and abundance of provision.

The second: it is contentment with what is easily available and patience with what is decreed.

The third: it is abandoning the creatures and turning to the Truth; this was said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah. It may also bear three aspects: One: it is lawful sufficiency.

The second: it is that which involves no toil or seeking.

The third: it is that which is coupled with health and well-being.

﴿until a specified term﴾ has three interpretations: (p-457) One: until the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: until the day of death; this was said by al-Hasan.

The third: until a time known only to Allah Most High; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿and will give every doer of virtue his virtue﴾ has two meanings. One: He guides him to righteous deeds; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: He rewards him for it in the Hereafter, according to the view of Qatadah.

It is also permissible that He rewards him for it in this world, according to the view of Mujahid.

﴿But if you turn away﴾ means from what you have been commanded.

﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ contains an implied supposition: "Then say to them: indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day," meaning the Day of Resurrection, described as such because of the greatness of the matters that occur in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Verily they fold their breasts to hide from Him⦆. Concerning this there are five opinions:

First: They fold their breasts over disbelief in order to hide from Allah, the Exalted. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: They fold them over enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ in order to conceal it from him. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Third: They fold them over what they harbor of inner thoughts (hadith al-nafs) in order to conceal it from people. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: The hypocrites, whenever they passed by the Prophet ﷺ, would cover their heads and fold their breasts so as to hide from him, so that he would not recognize them. This was said by Abu Razin.

Fifth: A man said, "When I close my door, draw my curtain, cover myself with my garment and fold my chest, who will know about me?" So Allah, the Exalted, informed them that He knows what they conceal and what they disclose.

﴿Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments⦆ means they wrap themselves in their clothes and cover themselves with them. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':

"I tend the stars, though I was not charged with their care, and at times I cover myself with the excess of my worn garments."

Concerning the meaning of ﴿when they cover themselves with their garments⦆ there are four opinions. First: it is the night, in which they intend to conceal their secrets through what they fold their breasts over. Allah, the Exalted, is not hidden from what they conceal at night nor from what they hide within their breasts. So He alluded to the night by their covering themselves with their garments, because they cover themselves with its darkness just as they cover themselves when they draw their garments over them.

Second: some of the disbelievers, out of their extreme hatred for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, would cover themselves with their garments, covering their faces with them and stopping their ears with them, so that they would neither see his person nor hear his speech. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

Third: some of the hypocrites would show the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with their tongues that they were obedient to him and loved him, while their hearts harbored hatred for him and disobedience to him. So He made what their hearts contained like one who is covered with his garment.

Fourth: some of the Muslims would practice asceticism by covering their bodies and not uncovering them under the sky. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear that the true devotion is what their hearts contain of belief and what they display of speech and action.

Then He explained this, saying: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they disclose⦆. Concerning this there are three aspects. First: what they conceal in their hearts and what they disclose with their mouths. Second: what they conceal of faith and what they disclose of acts of worship. Third: what they conceal of the deeds of the night and what they disclose of the deeds of the day. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts⦆: it was said, of the secrets of the breasts.

Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq al-Thaqafi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 6:

(p-459) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And He knows its resting place and its place of storage﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: its resting place is where it lodges, and its place of storage is where it dies.

The second: its resting place is in the womb, and its place of storage is in the loins (ṣulb), as said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The third: its resting place is in this world, and its place of storage is in the Hereafter.

It may also admit a fourth: that its resting place in the Hereafter is either Paradise or Hellfire, and its place of storage is in the heart, whether disbelief or faith.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 7–8:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. On this there are four interpretations:

First: that is, which of you is most complete in intellect (ʿaql). This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: which of you is most ascetic regarding this world. This is the saying of Sufyan.

Third: which of you is most thankful. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: what Kulayb ibn Wa'il narrated from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Which of you is best in deed? Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous in avoiding the prohibitions of Allah the Exalted, and quickest in obedience to Allah."

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a specified community﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

First: that is, until the perishing of a known community. This was mentioned by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

Second: until a counted term. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and the majority of the exegetes.

The word "ummah" here is an expression for a period of time; its original meaning is "community," but it is used to denote a period because the community lives within a period.

﴿They will surely say: What is it that holds it back?﴾ That is, the punishment.

Regarding their saying this, there are two interpretations:

First: they said this in denial of the punishment because of its delay in coming upon them.

Second: they said this in haste for the punishment and in mockery, meaning: what is it that has withheld it from us?

The Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then is he who has clear proof from his Lord﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions. The first: it is the Qur'an; this was said by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd.

The second: it is Muḥammad (ﷺ); this was said by Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, al-Sirrī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: it is the proofs that point to the Oneness of Allah the Exalted and the obligation of obeying Him; this was said by Ibn Baḥr.

Some of the Sufis mentioned a fourth opinion: that the clear proof is the insight into hearts and the wisdom regarding the unseen.

﴿And a witness from Him follows it﴾ — concerning this there are five opinions. The first: it is his tongue, which bears witness to him by reciting the Qur'an; this was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and from this is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"So do not think me a disbeliever in your favour, / Over my witness — O witness of Allah, then bear witness."

The second: it is Muḥammad (ﷺ), a witness from Allah the Exalted; this was said by ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn.

The third: it is Jibrīl (peace be upon him); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Nakhaʿī, ʿIkrimah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The fourth: it is ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him). al-Minhāl narrated from ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: ʿAlī said: "There is no one in Quraysh but that a verse was revealed concerning him." It was said to him: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: ﴿And a witness from Him follows it﴾.

The fifth: it is an angel who guards him; this was said by Mujāhid and Abu al-ʿĀliyah.

(p-462) It may also bear a sixth opinion: "and a witness from himself follows it," through knowledge of his proofs and evidences, which is his intellect and his oneness; said by Ibn Baḥr.

﴿And before it was the Book of Mūsā﴾ — concerning this there are two aspects. The first: before the Qur'an was the Book of Mūsā, which is the Torah; said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: before Muḥammad was the Book of Mūsā; said by Mujāhid.

﴿As a leader and a mercy﴾ — concerning this there are two aspects. The first: meaning, one who precedes us, and a mercy for them.

The second: a leader for the believers, due to their following what is in it, and a mercy for them.

﴿Those believe in it﴾ — meaning: those who are upon clear proof from their Lord and whom a witness from Him follows.

﴿But whoever disbelieves in it among the factions﴾ — concerning them there are two opinions. The first: they are the people of all religions, because they form factions; said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are those who formed factions against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), gathering to fight him.

Concerning who is meant by them there are three aspects. The first: Quraysh; said by al-Suddī.

The second: the Jews and the Christians; said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The third: the people of all religions.

﴿So the Fire is his promised place﴾ — meaning, it is his destination. Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:

"You brought them to the pools of death, gathered together, / So the Fire is their promised place, and death meets them."

﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾ — concerning this there are two aspects. The first: in doubt about the Qur'an; said by Muqātil.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ Its meaning: And who is more unjust to himself than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, by claiming that something was revealed to him when it was not revealed, or by denying what was revealed to him.

﴿Those will be presented before their Lord﴾. This is their gathering to the place of reckoning, like a commander's review of his army, except that the commander reviews them in order to see them, and this is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He, since He sees them before the gathering.

Second: it is the plural of shahid (witness) in the sense of shahid, like sharif (noble) and ashraf (nobles).

Regarding al-ashhad there are four sayings. First: they are the prophets, said by al-Dahhak. Second: they are the angels, said by Mujahid. Third: they are all creation, said by Qatadah. Fourth: the witnesses are four: the angels, the prophets, the believers, and the limbs, said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Who bar from the way of Allah﴾, meaning Quraysh.

i.e., for what his hands had earned.

i.e., the stab made them deserve anger.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 28:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: meaning, upon certainty from my Lord; this was said by Abu Imran al-Jawni.

The second: upon proof from my Lord; this was said by Ali ibn Isa.

(p-466) ﴿And He has given me mercy from Himself﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: faith.

The second: prophethood; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿But it has been made obscure to you﴾, meaning the clear evidence in His saying: ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾. He said ﴿it has been made obscure to you﴾ though it is they who were blind to it, because it was hidden from them by their neglect of reflection, so God blinded them to it.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs recited ﴿fa-'ummiyat 'alaykum﴾ with a dammah on the ʿayn and a shaddah on the mim. In the recitation of Ubayy it is fa-'ammaha, which agrees with the reading of those who recite with the dammah in the passive form whose subject is not named.

Regarding who made it obscure, on these two readings there are two interpretations. The first: that God Most High made it obscure to them.

The second: by the whispering of Satan.

And by what he adorned for them of falsehood, until they turned away from the truth.

The Prophet of God Noah, by this statement to his people, intended to answer their saying: ﴿And we see in you no superiority over us﴾, so as to show his superiority over them, in that he is upon clear evidence from his Lord and has been given mercy from Himself, while they have been deprived of that. What superiority is greater than this? Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Shall we compel you to it while you are averse to it?﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "Shall we compel you to the mercy?" This was said by Muqatil.

The second: "Shall we compel you to the evidence while you are averse to it?", and your acceptance of it is not valid while you are averse to it.

Qatadah said: By God, if the Prophet of God Noah, peace be upon him, had been able, he would have compelled it upon his people, but he did not have that power.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 31–34:

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And I do not say to you, "With me are the treasuries of Allah," nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say, "I am an angel."﴾ This statement of Nuh, peace be upon him, may have two interpretations. The first: it is a reply to his people based on their saying: ﴿We see you only as a human being like ourselves﴾. The second: it is a reply to them based on their saying: ﴿And we see no superiority of yours over us﴾. So Allah the Exalted said to him: "Say: ﴿And I do not say to you, 'With me are the treasuries of Allah'﴾." Concerning this there are two views. The first: it refers to mercy, meaning that the mercy is not in my hand so that I could bring it to you. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: it refers to wealth, meaning that I do not have wealth in my hand so that I could give you some of it in return for your faith.

﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾, so that I could inform you of what is in your souls.

﴿Nor do I say, "I am an angel"﴾, meaning, so that I would be separate from your kind.

(p-468) ﴿And I do not say to those whom your eyes despise, "Allah will never give them any good."﴾ Al-izdira'* means contempt.

It is said: "izdaraytu 'alayhi" when you find fault with him, and "zaraytu 'alayhi" when you belittle him.

Al-Mubarrad recited:

"His friend keeps him at a distance, and his wife holds him in contempt, and the young one drives him away."

﴿Allah will never give them any good﴾, meaning: your belittling of them does not nullify their reward or diminish their recompense. Likewise, by your elevated status in this world you do not gain more than your rewards.

﴿Allah knows best what is in their souls﴾, meaning: He will recompense them for it and hold them to account for it.

﴿Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: if I said what has been mentioned before.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 11, verses 36–39:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed.﴾ God, exalted is He, confirmed that their disbelief would continue, in order to make the threat against them come to pass. Al-Dahhak said: When he was informed of this, he prayed against them, saying: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. The first: "So do not grieve," and from this is the saying of Yazid ibn Abd al-Mudan:

*The horseman of horses, whenever the veiled maiden wailed with a voice full of distress.*

The second: "So do not grieve," and from this is the saying of the poet:

*And how many a friend or intimate has been struck by calamity, yet I did not grieve, though the calamity was great.*

Al-ibtiʼas (distress, grief accompanied by humility) is grief in a state of submissiveness, and it is derived from al-buʼs (misery). On this there are two views. The first: "Do not grieve over their destruction." The second: "Do not grieve over their disbelief, which leads to their destruction."

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes.﴾ On this there are three views. The first: "Within Our sight, where We see you," so the sight is expressed by "eyes" because sight occurs through them. The second: "With Our protection of you, the protection of one who sees you." The third: "With the eyes of Our angels, who are Our friends." It may also bear a fourth meaning: "With Our assistance to you in constructing it."

﴿And Our revelation﴾ has two meanings. The first: "And Our command to you to construct it." The second: "Our teaching you how to construct it."

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.﴾ God forbade him from pleading on their behalf, and His prohibition may carry two purposes. The first: to turn him away from asking for what will not be granted. The second: to turn away from him the sin of colluding with the tyrants.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship.﴾ Zayd ibn Aslam said: Noah, peace be upon him, remained for a hundred years planting trees, cutting them, and drying them, and for a hundred years working on it. Its dimensions were disputed in three opinions. The first is what al-Hasan said: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits, its width six hundred cubits, and it was covered over.

The second is what Ibn Abbas said: its length was four hundred cubits and its height thirty cubits.

Khusayf said: its length was three hundred cubits and its width fifty cubits. The birds were at its top, the people in its middle, and the beasts at its bottom.

It was launched from Ayn Warda on Friday, ten nights past the month of Rajab, and it came to rest at Baqardi upon al-Judi on the day of Ashura.

Qatada said: its door was in its side.

﴿Whenever a company of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him.﴾ On their ridiculing him there are two views. The first: they used to see him building a ship on dry land, so they mocked him, belittled him, and said: "O Noah, after prophethood you have become a carpenter!"

The second: when they saw him building the ship, and they had never witnessed a ship being built before, they said: "O Noah, what are you doing?" He said: "I am building a house that will walk upon the water," so they wondered at his words and ridiculed him.

﴿He said: If you ridicule us, then indeed we ridicule you as you ridicule.﴾ On this there are two views. The first: "If you ridicule our words, we will ridicule your heedlessness." The second: "If you ridicule our action today, in building the ship, then we will ridicule you tomorrow, at the drowning."

By ridicule here is meant treating as foolish (al-istijhal).

Its meaning is: "If you consider us foolish, then we consider you foolish."

Ibn Abbas said: Before the Flood there was no river or sea on the earth, and therefore they ridiculed him for it.

He said: The waters of the seas are a remnant of the Flood.

If it is asked: Why was it permissible to say, "indeed we ridicule you," given the ugliness of ridicule? It is answered: Because this is a rebuke which he made into a recompense for their ridicule, and he expressed it in this way to match the wording of the speech. Al-Zajjaj, because of this objection, interpreted it to mean: "If you consider us foolish, then indeed we consider you foolish, just as you consider us foolish."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water"﴾. He made the descent of the water into it equivalent to swallowing, and its meaning is: swallow the water that is upon you. Al-Hasan and al-Husayn, peace be upon them, related that some of the lands refused to swallow their water, so their water became bitter and their soil became saline (sabkha).

﴿And, "O sky, withhold"﴾, i.e., do not rain, from their saying aqla'a 'an al-shay' (he gave up the thing) when he left it.

﴿And the water subsided﴾, i.e., it decreased until its excess left the earth.

﴿And the matter was decided﴾, meaning by the destruction of those of the people of Noah who drowned.

﴿And it settled﴾, meaning the ship.

﴿On al-Judi﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: that it is a mountain in Mosul, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: that it is a mountain in al-Jazira, said by Mujahid.

Qatada said: It is at Baqarrdi (Baqardi), in the land of al-Jazira.

The third: that al-Judi is a name for every mountain, and from it is the verse of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl:

"Glory be to Him, then glory, which returns to Him, and before us al-Judi and al-Jumd glorified (Him)."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 45–47:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾. He said "of my family" because Allah Most High had promised him that He would save his family along with him.

﴿And indeed Your promise is the truth﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: it is that which is true (yaḥiqqu), so it is never broken. The second: it is that which is binding (yalzamu) just as truth is binding.

﴿And You are the most just of judges﴾ means, with the truth. From Noah this statement may admit of one of two matters: either it was before he knew of his son's drowning, so he asked Allah Most High for his deliverance; or it was after he knew of his drowning, so he asked Allah Most High for mercy for him.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family"﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: he was born on his (Noah's) bed but was not his son, and he was the son of another man, a ruling of legitimacy (rishda). This was said by al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid.

The second: he was the son of his wife.

The third: he was his son. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all."

It is also said that his name was Kanʿān, and it is said rather that his name was Yām.

Al-Ḥasan said: "He was a hypocrite, and for this reason Noah hastened to call out to him." Accordingly, in the interpretation of the words of the Most High, ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾, there are two meanings. The first: he is not of the people of your religion and your allegiance, and this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhūr). The second: he is not of your family whom I promised you I would save with you; this was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

﴿Indeed he is an unrighteous deed﴾ has three interpretations. The first: your asking me to save him is an unrighteous deed; this was said by Qatāda and Ibrāhīm, and it is the interpretation of those who read ﴿ʿamalun ghayru ṣāliḥin﴾ with tanwīn. 

The second: its meaning is that your son whom you asked me to save is an unrighteous deed, that is, he is of illegitimate birth; this was said by al-Ḥasan.

The third: that he is an unrighteous deed; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and it is the interpretation of those who do not read with tanwīn.

﴿So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: concerning what you attributed to yourself while he is not from you. The second: concerning his entry into the group of those whom I promised you I would save from your family, while he is not among them.

﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: from among the ignorant of your lineage. The second: from among the ignorant of My promise to you.

Regarding His saying, ﴿I admonish you﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "I am raising you above being among the ignorant." The second: its meaning is "I warn you," and from it is the saying of the Most High: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it⁠—ever﴾, that is, He warns you.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 48–52:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain⁠﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it is rain in its season, said by Harun al-Taymi.

The second: it is continuous rain, said by Ibn Abbas.

It may also bear two other meanings. The first: He causes it to flow when there is need. The second: He makes blessing flow through it, and this is derived from the flowing of milk from the udder.

﴿And He will add strength to your strength⁠﴾. Concerning this there are four views. The first: it means vigor added to your vigor, said by Mujahid.

The second: fertility added to your fertility, said by al-Dahhak.

The third: honor added to your honor through the abundance of your numbers and your wealth, said by Ali ibn Isa.

The fourth: that it is the child of the child, said by Ikrimah.

It may also bear a fifth meaning: He will add strength to you in your faith to your strength in your bodies.

"His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿He it is Who brought you into being from the earth﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: He created you from the earth, because you are descended from Adam, and Adam was from the earth. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Second: its meaning is that He brought you into being upon the earth.

Third: He brought you into being through the vegetation of the earth.

(p-479) ﴿And He settled you therein﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: its meaning is that He let you dwell therein (a'marakum) by placing you in it for the duration of your lifespans. This is the view of Mujahid, from the expression of people, "So-and-so granted so-and-so his house for life (umra), so it is his for life," (a'mara fulan fulanan darahu fa-hiya lahu 'umra).

Second: He commanded you to develop (i'mara) what you need therein, by building dwellings and planting trees. This is the view of Ali ibn Isa.

Third: He prolonged your deeds therein. This is the view of al-Dahhak, who said: your lifespans were a thousand years, up to three hundred years."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 62–63:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: i.e., one whom we had set our hopes upon, expecting your good.

The second: i.e., despised, from al-irja' (irja', meaning deferment or postponement). On the first interpretation it is a rebuke of complaint, and on the second it is a rebuke of reproach.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: upon a manifest truth. The second: upon an evident proof.

Al-Kalbi said: upon a religion from my Lord.

﴿And has given me mercy from Him﴾. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: he means prophethood and wisdom.

(p-480) ﴿So who will help me against Allah if I disobey Him?﴾ i.e., who will ward off from me the punishment of Allah if I disobey Him by obeying you?

﴿So you add nothing to me but loss﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: i.e., you add nothing to me in your argument of following your fathers except a loss that you yourselves suffer. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: you add nothing to me, with your rejection and denial, even if you were to respond to what you ask, except a loss through exchanging reward for punishment.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the Cry﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: that Jibril (peace be upon him) cried out at them.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 11, verses 69–73:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And Our messengers came to Ibrahim with good tidings﴾. As for Ibrahim, there are two views concerning it. The first: it is a non-Arabic name (ism a'jami), as said by most scholars.

It has also been said that its meaning is "a compassionate father."

(p-482) The second: it is an Arabic name derived from al-barhama (al-barhamah), which is prolonged gazing.

The messengers were Jibril, and with him were two angels. It has been said that they were Mika'il and Israfil, peace be upon them. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that the messengers who accompanied Jibril were twelve angels.

Concerning the good tidings with which they came to him, there are four sayings. The first: they gave him the good news of his prophethood, said by Ikrimah.

The second: the good news of Ishaq (Isaac), said by al-Hasan.

The third: they gave him the good news of the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ) from his loins, and that he is the Seal of the Prophets.

The fourth: they gave him the good news of the destruction of the people of Lut, said by Qatadah.

﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace."﴾ Concerning this there are two views. The first: it is a greeting from the angels to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and he returned the greeting with its like. This indicates that salam is the greeting of the angels and of the Muslims all together.

The second: "You and your family are safe from the destruction of the people of Lut."

His saying: ﴿Salam﴾, meaning "Praise be to God who has kept me safe." So the meaning of "salam" is "I am safe" (salimtu).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿سِلْمٌ﴾ (silm) with a kasrah on the sin and without the alif.

Scholars differed concerning silm and salam, on two views. The first: silm is from al-musalamah (peaceful relations), and salam is from al-salamah (safety).

The second: both have the same meaning. The poet, whom al-Farra' cited from one of the Arabs, said:

*We stood and said, "Ayh, peace (silm)!" and she responded with peace, as the bright clouds gather with lightning.*

﴿Then he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾. He thought that the messengers of his Lord were guests, because they came to him in human form, so he hastened to offer them hospitality, and he brought them a roasted calf (ʿijl hanidh).

Concerning hanidh there are two sayings. (p-483) The first: it means "hot," related by Aban ibn Taghlib from Alqamah al-Nahwi.

The second: it means "roasted thoroughly," and it is the same as mahnudh, like tabikh and matbukh. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it is that which is dug into the ground and then buried in it. The poet said:

*When we slaughter meat for the one who seeks hospitality, we heat it until its eater can see the meat clearly.*

The second: it is that which is placed over stones; when their heat becomes intense, it is put inside the animal's body so that it cooks quickly. Tarafah ibn al-Abd said:

*For them are wine and camphor and musk, and the wild game whose flesh is roasted (hanudh).*

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿When he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he found them strange (nakirahum)﴾. Concerning nakirahum and ankarahum there are two views. The first: their meanings differ. Nakirahum means he did not recognize them, and ankarahum means he found them in something disapproved.

The second: they have the same meaning. Al-A'sha said:

*She found me strange, and what she found strange was nothing but the gray hair and the baldness.*

Scholars differed about the reason for his finding them strange, on two views. The first: they did not eat. It is the custom of the Arabs that when a guest arrives and does not eat of their food, they suspect him of evil and fear harm from him. So Ibrahim found them strange for this reason, said by Qatadah.

The second: because they had no hands (that reached the food), so he found them strange, said by Yazid ibn Abi Habib.

They refrained from his food because they were angels, who neither eat nor drink.

﴿And he sensed fear of them﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: he concealed within himself fear of them.

The second: he perceived within himself a dread of them, as Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah said:

*The courier came with a paper hurriedly delivered, and the heart sensed dread from that paper.*

﴿They said, "Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut"﴾, meaning, for their destruction.

(p-484) Concerning their informing Ibrahim of this, there are two views. The first: so that his fear of them would be removed.

The second: because Ibrahim had been going to the people of Lut and saying, "Woe to you! Do you not forbid yourselves from God, so that you do not expose yourselves to His punishment?" But they did not obey him.

﴿And his wife was standing and laughed﴾. Concerning her standing, there are three sayings. The first: she was standing behind the curtain listening to their speech, said by Wahb.

The second: she was standing serving them, said by Mujahid.

The third: she was standing praying, said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

﴿Then she laughed﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: it means she menstruated, said by Mujahid. The Arabs say "the woman laughed" when she menstruates, and "al-dahk" (laughter) in their speech means menstruation. The poet said:

*The hares laughed upon the rock, like the blood of fear on the day of the encounter.*

The second: the meaning of "she laughed" is "she was astonished." Astonishment is sometimes called laughter because laughter arises from it. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*He brought a mixture such as people have never seen; it is laughter, except that it is the work of the bees.*

The third: it is the well-known laughter of the face, and this is the view of the majority.

If its interpretation is taken as menstruation, then concerning the cause of her menstruation there are two views. The first: it coincided with her customary time, and she feared that her blood would show and wanted to conceal it, so she was bewildered by the presence of the messengers.

The second: she was alarmed and frightened, so her menstruation came early, before its time. The customary period of menstruation may change according to circumstances and changes of temperament.

It may also bear a third view: that menstruation was a sign of the coming birth, because one who does not menstruate does not give birth.

If its interpretation is taken as astonishment, then concerning what she was astonished at there are four sayings. (p-485) The first: she was astonished that she and her husband were serving the guests out of honor for them, though they did not eat, said by al-Suddi.

The second: she was astonished that the punishment had come to the people of Lut while they were heedless, said by Qatadah.

The third: she was astonished that she should have a child at her old age and the old age of her husband, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: she was astonished at the bringing to life of the roasted calf, because Jibril, peace be upon him, had touched it with his wing, so it stood up, running until it reached its mother, and the mother of the calf was in the house, said by Awn ibn Abi Shaddad.

If its interpretation is taken as laughter of the face, then concerning what she laughed at there are four sayings. The first: she laughed out of joy at being safe.

The second: out of joy at the child.

The third: because she saw what her husband had of scrupulousness (wara'), said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: she laughed, thinking that the messengers would do the deed of the people of Lut, said by Muhammad ibn Isa.

﴿So We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾. Concerning "wara'" (after/behind) here, there are two views. The first: wara' means "the child was born after the child," said by Ibn Abbas and al-Sha'bi.

The second: it means "after" (ba'd), said by Muqatil. al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

*I swore, and I did not leave for you any doubt, and there is no path for a man beyond (wara') God.*

They hastened to give her the good news of two sons, as a manifestation of blessing and an exaggeration in astonishment. It is possible that the good news of the two was given by their names, so that God Himself would be the one who named them. It is also possible that the good news was of the two, and their father named them.

If it is asked: why was Sarah singled out for the good news rather than Ibrahim? It is answered that there are three replies. The first: because she was singled out for laughter, she was singled out for the good news.

(p-486) The second: they rewarded her with the good news in return for her great service.

The third: because women are greater in joy and more elated at the good news of a child.

Ibn Abbas said: Ishaq was named so because Sarah "sahuqat" (was made to laugh) when she was given the good news of him.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman, and this, my husband, is an old man?"﴾ She did not intend by her saying "woe to me" a supplication against herself with woe, but it is a phrase that comes easily to the mouths of women when something befalls them that they wonder at. She was astonished at giving birth while she was old and her husband was an old man, because this departs from the custom. What departs from custom is strange and considered unusual.

There was disagreement about her age and the age of Ibrahim at that time. Mujahid said: Sarah was ninety-nine years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred years old.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Sarah was ninety years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred and twenty years old.

Qatadah said: each of them was ninety years old.

It has also been said that by her saying ﴿and this, my husband, is an old man﴾ she was alluding to his abstaining from intimacy with her. "Ba'l" here means "husband," as in God's saying: ﴿and their husbands (bu'ulatuhunna) have the better right to take them back in that period﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. "Ba'l" also means "a deity that is worshipped," as in God's saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l?﴾ [al-Saffat: 125], meaning a god that is worshipped.

"Ba'l" also means "master," as in the saying of Labid:

*With their brocade sleeves bared at their arms, before a master (ba'l) of firm judgment and courage.*

So the husband was called "ba'l" because of his superiority over the wife, as the master's superiority over the one mastered.

﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing (shay'un 'ajib)﴾, meaning "something disapproved," and God's saying: ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2] is of the same usage, meaning they found it strange.

This was not from her a denial, but a finding it strange.

The second: the meaning of "she laughed" is "she was astonished." Astonishment is sometimes called laughter because laughter arises from it. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*He brought a mixture such as people have never seen; it is laughter, except that it is the work of the bees.*

The third: it is the well-known laughter of the face, and this is the view of the majority.

If its interpretation is taken as menstruation, then concerning the cause of her menstruation there are two views. The first: it coincided with her customary time, and she feared that her blood would show and wanted to conceal it, so she was bewildered by the presence of the messengers.

The second: she was alarmed and frightened, so her menstruation came early, before its time. The customary period of menstruation may change according to circumstances and changes of temperament.

It may also bear a third view: that menstruation was a sign of the coming birth, because one who does not menstruate does not give birth.

If its interpretation is taken as astonishment, then concerning what she was astonished at there are four sayings. (p-485) The first: she was astonished that she and her husband were serving the guests out of honor for them, though they did not eat, said by al-Suddi.

The second: she was astonished that the punishment had come to the people of Lut while they were heedless, said by Qatadah.

The third: she was astonished that she should have a child at her old age and the old age of her husband, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: she was astonished at the bringing to life of the roasted calf, because Jibril, peace be upon him, had touched it with his wing, so it stood up, running until it reached its mother, and the mother of the calf was in the house, said by Awn ibn Abi Shaddad.

If its interpretation is taken as laughter of the face, then concerning what she laughed at there are four sayings. The first: she laughed out of joy at being safe.

The second: out of joy at the child.

The third: because she saw what her husband had of scrupulousness (wara'), said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: she laughed, thinking that the messengers would do the deed of the people of Lut, said by Muhammad ibn Isa.

﴿So We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾. Concerning "wara'" (after/behind) here, there are two views. The first: wara' means "the child was born after the child," said by Ibn Abbas and al-Sha'bi.

The second: it means "after" (ba'd), said by Muqatil. al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

*I swore, and I did not leave for you any doubt, and there is no path for a man beyond (wara') God.*

They hastened to give her the good news of two sons, as a manifestation of blessing and an exaggeration in astonishment. It is possible that the good news of the two was given by their names, so that God Himself would be the one who named them. It is also possible that the good news was of the two, and their father named them.

If it is asked: why was Sarah singled out for the good news rather than Ibrahim? It is answered that there are three replies. The first: because she was singled out for laughter, she was singled out for the good news.

(p-486) The second: they rewarded her with the good news in return for her great service.

The third: because women are greater in joy and more elated at the good news of a child.

Ibn Abbas said: Ishaq was named so because Sarah "sahuqat" (was made to laugh) when she was given the good news of him.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman, and this, my husband, is an old man?"﴾ She did not intend by her saying "woe to me" a supplication against herself with woe, but it is a phrase that comes easily to the mouths of women when something befalls them that they wonder at. She was astonished at giving birth while she was old and her husband was an old man, because this departs from the custom. What departs from custom is strange and considered unusual.

There was disagreement about her age and the age of Ibrahim at that time. Mujahid said: Sarah was ninety-nine years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred years old.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Sarah was ninety years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred and twenty years old.

Qatadah said: each of them was ninety years old.

It has also been said that by her saying ﴿and this, my husband, is an old man﴾ she was alluding to his abstaining from intimacy with her. "Ba'l" here means "husband," as in God's saying: ﴿and their husbands (bu'ulatuhunna) have the better right to take them back in that period﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. "Ba'l" also means "a deity that is worshipped," as in God's saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l?﴾ [al-Saffat: 125], meaning a god that is worshipped.

"Ba'l" also means "master," as in the saying of Labid:

*With their brocade sleeves bared at their arms, before a master (ba'l) of firm judgment and courage.*

So the husband was called "ba'l" because of his superiority over the wife, as the master's superiority over the one mastered.

﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing (shay'un 'ajib)﴾, meaning "something disapproved," and God's saying: ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2] is of the same usage, meaning they found it strange.

This was not from her a denial, but a finding it strange.

(p-487) His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿So when the fear had left Abraham﴾, i.e. the fright. Al-raw' (الرُّوع) with a dammah on the ra' means the soul (al-nafs), and from it comes the expression "alqa fi raw'i" (it was cast into my soul / into my mind), meaning "in my soul."

﴿And good news had come to him﴾, i.e. of Isaac and Jacob.

﴿He argued with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾. There are three interpretations regarding this:

The first: he argued with the angels through his saying: ﴿Indeed, Lot is therein.﴾ They said: ﴿We know best who is therein; we will surely save him and his family﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 32]. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri).

The second: he asked them, "Will you punish them if there are fifty believers in it?" They said, "No." He said, "What if there are forty?" They said, "No." He continued until he brought it down to ten, and they said, "No." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: he asked them about their punishment, whether it was the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal), which would certainly befall them, as a means of warning so that they might believe. This was his argument with them, and although it was a question, it came out in the form of uncovering something obscure.

Abu Malik said: None believed in Lot except his two daughters, Ruqayyah, who was the elder, and 'Arubah, who was the younger.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 77–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was troubled on their account and felt constrained for them⟩. Ibn ʿAbbas said: his opinion of his people became bad, and he felt constrained on account of his guests.

It may also bear another meaning: that he thought ill of the messengers of his Lord, and felt constrained for the sake of his own safety, because he disliked them before knowing them.

﴿And he said, "This is a distressing day."⟩ That is, a severe one, because he feared for the messengers from his people that they would disgrace them, according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. And according to the possibility I have mentioned, he feared for himself, so he described his day as ʿaṣīb, which means severe. The poet said: (p-488)

؎ If you do not accept Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a day in Iraq that is ʿaṣīb.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it was called ʿaṣīb because it binds (yaʿṣibu) people with evil. Al-Kalbi said: the distance between the village of Ibrahim and the people of Lut was four farsakh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his people came rushing toward him⟩, that is, they hastened. Al-ihrāʿ (rushing) lies between running (al-harwala) and a brisk walk (al-ḥujzā).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: ihrāʿ is only hastening with trembling.

The reason for their hastening to him was that Lut's wife informed them about his guests and their beauty, so they hastened to him seeking immorality from them.

﴿And before this they had been doing evil deeds⟩. There are two views concerning this. One: before their hastening to him, they had been having intercourse with males; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: the practice of sodomy among the people of Lut was with women before men, by forty years; this was said by ʿUmar ibn Abi Za'ida.

﴿He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you."⟩ Lut said this to them in order to ransom his guests from them.

﴿These are my daughters⟩. Concerning them there are two views. One: he meant the women of his community and did not mean his own daughters.

Mujahid said: every prophet is a father to his community, and they are his children.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: in some recitation of the Qur'an: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."

The second: he meant his own daughters and the children of his loins, because his command over them was more binding than his command over others; this is the meaning of the saying of Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman.

If it is said: how could he marry them to them while his people were disbelievers and his daughters were believers? It is answered that there are three responses concerning this. One: in the law of Lut it was permissible to marry a believing woman to a disbeliever, and this was permissible in the early period of Islam until it was abrogated; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he would marry them to them on condition of faith, as is stipulated in the contract of marriage.

The third: he said that to encourage what is lawful and to draw attention to what is permitted, and to prevent haste without offering their marriage or proposing to them; this was said by Ibn Abi Najih.

(p-489) ﴿They are purer for you⟩, that is, more lawful for you through valid marriage.

﴿So fear God and do not disgrace me regarding my guests⟩. Concerning this there are three meanings. One: do not humiliate me with the shame of disgrace, the word khizy here meaning humiliation.

The second: do not destroy me through the consequences of your corruption, the word khizy here meaning destruction.

The third: the meaning of khizy here is modesty (istiḥyāʾ); it is said khaziya al-rajul when he felt shame. The poet said:

؎ Of the fair-skinned women who are not ashamed when the wind clings their shawl to them, or when the jewelry slips from their necks.

Al-day̆f (the guest) is the visitor who seeks lodging; it applies to one and to many. The poet said:

؎ Do not let the blades of the butcher ever be lacking for the guest, for the guest is the most deserving visitor.

﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?⟩ Concerning this there are two meanings. One: that is, a believer; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: one who enjoins good and forbids evil; this was said by Abu Malik.

It means: a man of sound judgment who would repel (harm) from his guests, and he said this in astonishment at their gathering upon wrongdoing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "You know well that we have no right to your daughters; and indeed you know what we want."⟩ Concerning this there are two meanings. One: we have no need of them; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: we have no husbands among them; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

﴿And indeed you know what we want⟩. Concerning this there are two meanings. One: you know that we do not marry except a single woman, and there is not among us a man who does not have a wife; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: that we want men. (p-490)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 80–81:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in some strong support!"﴾ He means: supporters.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He meant offspring.

﴿Or could take refuge in some strong support﴾ means: in a protecting tribe (ʿashīrah māniʿah).

Abu Salamah narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lot; he used to take refuge in a strong support." He meant Allah, exalted is He. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah did not send any prophet after him except among a numerous people." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The messengers were fond of Lot and said: "Indeed your support is strong."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you."﴾ Regarding his name there are two views. The first: it is a non-Arabic name, and this is the view of most scholars.

The second: it is an Arabic name, derived from their saying: "I smoothed (lattu) the basin" (lantu al-hawd), when you smooth it with clay (idha mallastahu bil-tin).

It was also said that Lot was standing at his door, preventing his people from his guests. When they informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, he allowed his people to enter, and Jibril (peace be upon him) wiped over their eyes so they were blinded, and over their hands so they dried up.

﴿So travel with your family﴾ means: go with your family by night. Al-suraa is travel by night. ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah said:

"At dawn the people praise the night journey, and the drowsy haze clears away from them."

It is said both "asrā" and "sarā," and regarding them there are two views. The first: their meaning in traveling by night is one. The second: their meanings differ; asrā is to travel from the beginning of the night, and sarā is to travel in its last part, and in the daytime only sāra is used. Labid said:

"When a man travels by night, he thinks he has accomplished a deed, yet a man, as long as he lives, is a worker."

﴿At a portion of the night﴾: concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: its meaning is the darkness of the night, said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the middle of the night, derived from dividing it into two halves, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a wailing woman who wails in a portion of the night, over a man on the stony ground."

The third: it is the first dawn, said by Humayd ibn Ziyad.

The fourth: it is a part of the night, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And let none of you look back﴾: concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: none of you should look behind him, said by Mujahid.

The second: it means none of you should lag behind, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it means none of you should busy himself with what he leaves behind of property or possessions, related by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿Except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them﴾: concerning it there are two views. The first: his saying ﴿except your wife﴾ is an exception from his saying: "So travel with your family by a portion of the night, except your wife." This is the view of those who read ﴿except your wife﴾ with a fatha (accusative).

The second: it is an exception from his saying: ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾, and it carries the sense of a substitute (badal) when it is read with a damma (nominative).

﴿Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them﴾: Qatadah mentioned that she went out with Lot from the town, heard the noise, and turned around, so Allah sent a stone upon her and destroyed her.

﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾ It was reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When Lot knew that they were messengers of his Lord, he said: 'Then now, indeed,' and Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾." It is also permissible that He made the morning the appointed time for their destruction, because souls are most deposited (at rest) in it and people are most gathered in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 80–81:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in some strong support!"﴾ He means: supporters.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He meant offspring.

﴿Or could take refuge in some strong support﴾ means: in a protecting tribe (ʿashīrah māniʿah).

Abu Salamah narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lot; he used to take refuge in a strong support." He meant Allah, exalted is He. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah did not send any prophet after him except among a numerous people." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The messengers were fond of Lot and said: "Indeed your support is strong."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you."﴾ Regarding his name there are two views. The first: it is a non-Arabic name, and this is the view of most scholars.

The second: it is an Arabic name, derived from their saying: "I smoothed (lattu) the basin" (lantu al-hawd), when you smooth it with clay (idha mallastahu bil-tin).

It was also said that Lot was standing at his door, preventing his people from his guests. When they informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, he allowed his people to enter, and Jibril (peace be upon him) wiped over their eyes so they were blinded, and over their hands so they dried up.

﴿So travel with your family﴾ means: go with your family by night. Al-suraa is travel by night. ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah said:

"At dawn the people praise the night journey, and the drowsy haze clears away from them."

It is said both "asrā" and "sarā," and regarding them there are two views. The first: their meaning in traveling by night is one. The second: their meanings differ; asrā is to travel from the beginning of the night, and sarā is to travel in its last part, and in the daytime only sāra is used. Labid said:

"When a man travels by night, he thinks he has accomplished a deed, yet a man, as long as he lives, is a worker."

﴿At a portion of the night﴾: concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: its meaning is the darkness of the night, said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the middle of the night, derived from dividing it into two halves, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a wailing woman who wails in a portion of the night, over a man on the stony ground."

The third: it is the first dawn, said by Humayd ibn Ziyad.

The fourth: it is a part of the night, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And let none of you look back﴾: concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: none of you should look behind him, said by Mujahid.

The second: it means none of you should lag behind, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it means none of you should busy himself with what he leaves behind of property or possessions, related by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿Except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them﴾: concerning it there are two views. The first: his saying ﴿except your wife﴾ is an exception from his saying: "So travel with your family by a portion of the night, except your wife." This is the view of those who read ﴿except your wife﴾ with a fatha (accusative).

The second: it is an exception from his saying: ﴿And let none of you look back, except your wife﴾, and it carries the sense of a substitute (badal) when it is read with a damma (nominative).

﴿Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them﴾: Qatadah mentioned that she went out with Lot from the town, heard the noise, and turned around, so Allah sent a stone upon her and destroyed her.

Is not the morning near?﴾." It is also permissible that He made the morning the appointed time for their destruction, because souls are most deposited (at rest) in it and people are most gathered in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 82–83:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿When Our command came﴾ — concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: it is the command of Allah Most High to the angels. The second: it is the descent of the punishment upon them. The third: it is the decree of their punishment.

﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: Allah Most High sent Jibril to the overturned settlements of the people of Lut. He lifted them on his wing and ascended with them until the people of the heavens could hear the barking of their dogs and the crowing of their roosters. Then he overturned them, making their highest part their lowest, and sent after them stones of sijjil, until he destroyed them and what was around them. There were five of them: Sabgha, Muqirra, Umra, Dawm, and Sadum, which is the greatest town.

Qatada said: They were in three towns called Sadum, between Madina and Syria, and there were four thousand thousand (four million) in them.

﴿And We rained down upon them stones of sijjil﴾. Concerning it there are eight interpretations. The first: it is a Persian word, arabized, and it is (sink and keil). Sink means stone and keil means clay. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is clay that has been baked until it became like millstones. This was mentioned by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: it is hard, strong stones. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited the verse of Ibn Muqbil: (p-493)

"A journey in which they strike the white swords sideways, a striking that the heroes enjoined upon one another, sijjinan."

However, the nun was changed to lam.

The fourth: "of sijjil" means "from a sky whose name is Sijjil." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: "of sijjil" means "from Jahannam," whose name is Sijjin, and the nun was changed to lam.

The sixth: that sijjil is from al-sijill, which is the book. Its meaning is: of the written stones which Allah Most High decreed to punish with, or which He had written upon. In the revelation: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7–9].

The seventh: that it is fi'il from al-sijl, which is sending. It is said "asjaltuhu," meaning "I sent him." From this the bucket is called sajl because of its being sent down. So al-sijl is the one sent upon them.

The eighth: that it is derived from al-sijl, which is a gift. It is said "sajjaltu lahu sajlan min al-'ata'," so it is as if He said: "Be granted the trial," meaning: give it to them.

﴿Manduad﴾ (piled up, layered): concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: some of it was arranged upon other parts, said by al-Rabi'. The second: arranged in rows, said by Qatada.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Marked from your Lord﴾. Al-musawwama means the marked, derived from al-simaa, which is the sign. The poet said:

"A youth whom Allah endowed with beauty while still a youth, having a mark that does not trouble the sight."

Concerning its sign there are two views. The first: that they were sealed, with the name of its owner upon each stone. The second: marked with whiteness over redness, according to Ibn 'Abbas. Qatada said: encircled with blackness over redness.

﴿From your Lord﴾: concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: in the knowledge of your Lord, said by Ibn Bahr. The second: in the treasuries of your Lord, which no one else possesses, and no one disposes of them except by His command.

﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾: concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: He mentioned it as a warning to the wrongdoers of Quraysh, said by Mujahid. The second: a warning to the wrongdoers of the Arabs, said by Ikrima. The third: a warning to the wrongdoers of this Ummah, said by Qatada. The fourth: a warning to every wrongdoer, said by al-Rabi'.

Concerning the stones that were rained down there are two views. The first: they were rained upon the cities when He lifted them up. The second: they were rained upon those of its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 84:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾ Madyan are the people of Shu'ayb. Regarding their being named thus, there are two opinions:

First: because they are the sons of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, so it is said "Madyan," and what is meant is "the sons of Madyan," just as it is said "Mudar" and what is meant is "the sons of Mudar."

Second: that Madyan is the name of their city, so they were attributed to it, and then only the name of the city was used, for brevity.

Then there are two views concerning it. The first: that it is a non-Arabic (a'jami) name.

The second: that it is an Arabic name, and regarding its derivation there are two views. The first: that it is from their saying "madana bi-l-makan" (he resided in the place) when he stayed in it, and the yā' is extra. This is the view of those who hold that it is the name of a city.

(p-495) The second: that it is derived from their saying "dayantu," meaning "I possessed/ruled," and the mīm is extra. This is the view of those who hold that it is the name of a man.

As for Shu'ayb, it is the diminutive of sha'b, and concerning it there are three views. The first: that it is the path in the mountain.

The second: that it is a great tribe.

The third: that it is derived from the "sha'b" (crack) of a broken vessel.

﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance.﴾ They, along with their disbelief, were people of cheating and fraud (bakhs wa tatfif), so they were commanded to believe, as a turning away from polytheism, and to give full measure, as a prohibition of fraud.

﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: that he meant cheapness of prices, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: that it is wealth and the adornment of this world, said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

And it may bear a third interpretation: that it is abundance and gain.

﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day﴾ In this there are three interpretations. The first: the high price of goods, which is what the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan implies.

The second: the punishment of annihilation in this world.

The third: the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 85–86:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿What remains from Allah is better for you, if you are believers﴾. Regarding it there are six sayings:

First: it means that obedience to Allah Most High is better for you. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: it is a charge from Allah. This was said by al-Rabi'.

Third: it is the mercy of Allah. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: your portion from your Lord is better for you. This was said by Qatadah.

Fifth: the provision of Allah is better for you. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-496) Sixth: what Allah leaves for you after you give people their rights by the measure and the balance is better for you. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾ may bear three meanings. First: a guardian protecting you from the punishment of Allah Most High reaching you.

Second: a guardian over the blessings of Allah Most High, lest they depart from you.

Third: a guardian protecting you from diminishing (al-bakhs) and cheating (al-tatfif) if you do not obey your Lord in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 87:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer order you that we leave what our fathers worshipped"﴾. Regarding ﴿your prayer﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: your recitation (qira'ah). This was said by al-A'mash.

The second: your prayer which you perform to Allah in worship (ta'abbud).

The third: your religion (din) which you hold to and have been commanded to follow, because the origin of prayer (salah) is following (ittiba'), and from it comes the rider (musalli) of horses, i.e., the one who follows closely behind.

﴿Does order you﴾ has two meanings. The first: it calls you to our affair (amr).

The second: in it is that you command us to leave what our fathers worshipped, meaning the idols and images.

﴿Or that we do with our wealth what we wish﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: what they were upon of defrauding (bakhs) and cheating in measure (tatfif).

The second: zakah. He used to command them to pay it, and they would refrain from it. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan al-Thawri.

The third: clipping dirhams and dinars, because he used to forbid them from it. Zayd ibn Aslam said this.

﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: they said this mockingly toward him. This was said by Qatadah.

(p-497) The second: its meaning is that you are neither forbearing nor rightly guided, in the sense of negation. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they acknowledged him as forbearing and rightly guided in its true sense, and said: "You are forbearing and rightly guided, so why do you forbid us from doing with our wealth what we wish?" Forbearance and right guidance do not require preventing the owner from doing what he wishes with his property. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 88:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾. We have already mentioned its interpretation (ta'wil).

﴿and He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: it is lawful wealth; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Ibn Abbas said: Shu'ayb was a man of abundant wealth.

The second: it is prophethood. This was mentioned by Ibn Isa. In the speech there is an omission, and its implied meaning is: "Would I then turn away from His worship with all that?"

Then he said: ﴿and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from.﴾ That is, I do not do what I have forbidden you, just as I do not abandon what I have commanded you.

﴿I intend only reform, as far as I am able﴾. Its meaning: I intend only to do what is righteous as far as I am able, because capability (istita'ah) is a condition of the act, not of the intention.

﴿And my success is only through Allah; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back in repentance﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: inabah (turning back) means return, and the meaning is "and to Him I return"; this was said by Mujahid. The second: inabah means supplication, and the meaning is "and to Him I call upon"; this was said by Ubayd Allah ibn Ya'la.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 89–90:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition (shiqaq) bring upon you⌉ the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾. Regarding ﴿yajrimannakum﴾ (bring upon you / cause you to incur) there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "let not ... carry you", said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: its meaning is "let not ... earn for you", said by al-Zajjaj.

And regarding His saying ﴿shiqaqi﴾ (my opposition) there are three interpretations. The first: my harming (idrari), said by al-Hasan. The second: my enmity (adawati), said by al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

Is there no one to convey to Qays a message, so how did you find the taste of shiqaq (enmity)?

The third: my separation (firaqi), said by Qatadah.

﴿That there befall you the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾, and they were the first nation to be destroyed with punishment.

﴿Or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lut are not far from you﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: it means the distance of the abode, due to their nearness to them, said by Qatadah. The second: the distance of time due to the nearness of the era.

It may be intended that it refers to both nearness of abode and nearness of time.

The people of Hud were destroyed by the violent wind, the people of Salih by the quake and the blast, and the people of Lut by stoning.

(p-499) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say"﴾ — that is, we do not comprehend it. From this, the knowledge of religion is called fiqh (jurisprudence, understanding), because it is something understood. On this there are two views:

The first: "We do not understand the soundness of what you say regarding futility and recompense."

The second: they said this out of aversion to listening to him and contempt for his speech.

﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾ — on this there are seven interpretations:

The first: weak of sight. This is the view of Sufyan.

The second: weak of body. Related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: blind. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

The fourth: little knowledge, and solitary. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: humiliated and contemptible. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The sixth: little intellect.

The seventh: little knowledge of the affairs of this world and of managing its people.

﴿Were it not for your clan﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: your tribe. This is the view of the majority.

The second: were it not for your followers. Related by al-Naqqash.

﴿we would have stoned you﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: we would have killed you by stoning.

The second: we would have reviled you with words. From this is the verse of al-Ja'di: (p-500)

"We exchanged bitter words until we became like two horses racing."

﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: not honored.

The second: not invulnerable, were it not for your clan.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah?"﴾ — that is, you regard my clan concerning me, and you do not regard Allah concerning me.

﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs〔ẓihriyyan〕﴾ — on this there are four interpretations:

The first: you have cast His command behind your backs, not turning to it nor acting upon it. This is the view of al-Suddi. From this is the verse of the poet:

"... ... ... ... We found the sons of al-Barsa'* among the offspring of the back" — that is, among those who are not regarded or given weight.

The second: meaning that you have carried the burdens of opposing Him upon your backs. This is the view of al-Suddi, from the saying "I carried so-and-so upon my back" when you display his hostility.

The third: meaning that you have made Allah a thing behind the back: if you need Him, you seek His help, and if you are content, you leave Him. Like the camel-driver who takes his camel as a thing behind the back: if he needs it, he loads it, and if he is independent of it, he abandons it. This is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that Allah Most High has made them, behind their backs, a thing cast aside. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾ — on this there are three views: (p-501)

The first: Preserver (ḥafīẓ).

The second: All-Aware (khabīr).

The third: Recompenser (mujāzin).

The first: weak of sight. This is the view of Sufyan.

The second: weak of body. Related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: blind. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

The fourth: little knowledge, and solitary. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: humiliated and contemptible. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The sixth: little intellect.

The seventh: little knowledge of the affairs of this world and of managing its people.

﴿Were it not for your clan﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: your tribe. This is the view of the majority.

The second: were it not for your followers. Related by al-Naqqash.

﴿we would have stoned you﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: we would have killed you by stoning.

The second: we would have reviled you with words. From this is the verse of al-Ja'di: (p-500)

"We exchanged bitter words until we became like two horses racing."

﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾ — on this there are two views:

The first: not honored.

The second: not invulnerable, were it not for your clan.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah?"﴾ — that is, you regard my clan concerning me, and you do not regard Allah concerning me.

﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs〔ẓihriyyan〕﴾ — on this there are four interpretations:

The first: you have cast His command behind your backs, not turning to it nor acting upon it. This is the view of al-Suddi. From this is the verse of the poet:

"... ... ... ... We found the sons of al-Barsa'* among the offspring of the back" — that is, among those who are not regarded or given weight.

The second: meaning that you have carried the burdens of opposing Him upon your backs. This is the view of al-Suddi, from the saying "I carried so-and-so upon my back" when you display his hostility.

The third: meaning that you have made Allah a thing behind the back: if you need Him, you seek His help, and if you are content, you leave Him.
