The fourth: that Allah Most High has made them, behind their backs, a thing cast aside. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾ — on this there are three views: (p-501)

The first: Preserver (ḥafīẓ).

The second: All-Aware (khabīr).

The third: Recompenser (mujāzin).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 93–95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, act according to your standing﴾. In this there are two views. The first: according to your situation (naahiyah), as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: according to your firmly established condition (tamakkun), as said by Ibn Isa.

His saying: ﴿act﴾ means what they had promised him of destroying him. He said this out of confidence in his Lord.

Then He said, as a reply to them, containing threat and warning: ﴿Indeed, I am acting. You are going to know﴾. In this there are two views. The first: you will know the answer (to the supplication).

The second: I am acting regarding the matter of the one who will come to destroy you, so that He may purify the earth of you, and you will see the descent of punishment upon you.

﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾. Ikrimah said: it is drowning.

And regarding ﴿will disgrace him﴾ there are two views. The first: it humiliates him.

The second: it exposes him.

﴿And who is a liar﴾. In this there is an omitted, implied element, its estimate being: and who is a liar will be disgraced by the punishment of Allah. He omitted it, being content with the sense of the speech.

﴿And wait﴾, meaning, await the punishment.

﴿Indeed, I am with you a watcher﴾. This may bear two meanings. The first: Indeed, I am with you a witness.

(p-502) The second: Indeed, I am with you a guarantor.

And there is a third view in it: Indeed, I am awaiting, as said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 96–99:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

The first: the curse in this world is from the believers, and in the Hereafter it is from the angels.

The second: by the curse of this world he meant drowning, and by the curse of the Hereafter the Fire. This was said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾. There are three opinions regarding this:

The first: "wretched is the aid that is aided." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The third: al-Rifd means increase, and its meaning is "wretched is what they are given as increase after the drowning: the Fire." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 100–101:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿That is among the tidings of the towns which We relate to you﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it: The first: We inform you of it. The second: We cause some of it to follow others.

﴿Of them some are standing and some are reaped﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it: The first: that "standing" refers to the inhabited towns, and "reaped" refers to the desolate ones. This is what Ibn Abbas said.

(p-503) The second: that "standing" refers to the traces, and "reaped" refers to the effaced. This is what Qatadah said. The poet said:

"And people, in the apportioning of death among them, are like crops: of it some are standing and some are reaped."

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And they did not increase them except in ruin (tatbib)﴾. There are three interpretations regarding it: The first: that tatbib is evil. This is what Ibn Zayd said.

The second: that it is destruction. This is what Qatadah said. Labid said:

"Indeed I have worn out, and every companion of freshness [wears out] to a decay that returns, and that is tatbib."

From it is the saying of Jarir:

"A remnant of the people of Lut, so woe (tabban) to what they did, a woe (tababan)."

The third: that it is ruin (al-takhsir), which is loss (al-khusran). This is what Mujahid said, and he interpreted the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1] to mean: they have been lost.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations (ta'wilat, plural of ta'wil, "interpretation"):

First: No one will intercede except by His permission.

Second: No one will speak except what is permitted of good speech, because they will be compelled to abandon what is ugly.

Third: On the Day of Resurrection there is a time during which they are prevented from speaking, except by His permission.

﴿Among them are the wretched (shaqiyy) and the blessed (sa'id)﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

One: Among them are the deprived and the provided for. This is what Ibn Bahr said.

Second: Among them are the punished and the honoured. Labid said:

*Among them is the blessed one, taking his portion,*
*and among them is the wretched one, content with his livelihood.*

Then, concerning wretchedness and blessedness, there are two sayings:

One: God Most High made that a recompense for their deeds, so He blesses the obedient and makes the disobedient wretched. This is what Ibn Bahr said.

Second: God originated both wretchedness and blessedness for them without any recompense.

It is narrated by Abdullah ibn Umar, from his father, that he said: "When ﴿Among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾ was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of God, then on what do we act? On something already finished, or on what has not yet been finished?' He said: '(Rather, on something already finished, O Umar, over which the pens have run. But every person is made easy for that for which he was created.)'"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 106–107:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: al-zafir (groaning) is a loud sound, and al-shahiq (wailing) is a weak sound. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: al-zafir is in the throat, from the intensity of grief, and it is derived from al-zafir (the exhalation of a breath through the throat), while al-shahiq is in the chest. This is related from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

The third: al-zafir is the repeated drawing of breath from the intensity of grief, derived from al-zafr, which means carrying a load on the back because of its heaviness, and al-shahiq is a long, drawn-out breath, derived from their saying "jabal shahiq," meaning tall. This is related from Ibn ʿIsa.

The fourth: al-zafir is the beginning of a donkey's bray, and al-shahiq is its end. The poet said:

*He rasped in the belly, a sighing sound, or he gasped until one would say, "A braying one," though he had not brayed.*

﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning this there are eight interpretations. The first: they will abide therein for as long as the lowest heaven and its earth endure, except what your Lord wills of addition beyond the passing of their duration. This is related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: for as long as the heavens and earth of the Hereafter endure, except what your Lord wills of the length of their standing on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The third: for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, meaning the period of their stay in the world. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The fourth: they will abide therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills concerning the people of monotheism, that He brings them out of it after they have been made to enter it. This was said by Qatadah, so they will be wretched in the Fire and happy in the Garden. It is related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Yazid ibn Abi Habib narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Some people will enter Hell until, when they have become like charcoal, they will be taken out of it and admitted to the Garden, and it will be said, 'These are the people of Hell.'"

The fifth: except what He wills concerning the people of monotheism, that He does not make them enter it. This was said by Abu Nadrah, who transmits it as a report traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The sixth: except what your Lord wills concerning everyone who enters the Fire, whether a monotheist or a polytheist, that He brings him out of it when He wills. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The seventh: the exception refers to their saying, ﴿they will have therein groaning and wailing﴾, except what your Lord wills of kinds of punishment which are neither groaning nor wailing, of what has not been named or described, and of what has been named and described. Then He begins anew with ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. This is related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The eighth: the exception is made in the sense of: If your Lord willed not to make them abide forever, He would do so; but what He wills, desires, and decrees is that they abide forever.

Regarding the estimation of their abiding by the duration of the heavens and the earth there are two views. One: they are the heavens and earth of this world, and although they are perishable, they are, in the view of the Arabs, like what endures forever; so this was mentioned according to their custom and usage, as Zuhayr said:

*Behold, I see nothing enduring among the calamities, nor anything eternal except the firm mountains.*

The second view: they are the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, because they endure forever.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 108:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And as for those who are made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. In this verse there are five interpretations (ta'wilat):

First: "As long as the heavens and the earth of this world endure, except what your Lord wills" refers to an addition to their abiding therein.

Second: "Except what your Lord wills" refers to the duration of the Day of Resurrection.

Third: "Except what your Lord wills" refers to the length of their stay in the Fire until they come out of it. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: "Abiding therein" means the people of monotheism (ahl al-tawhid), and "except what your Lord wills" means the people of polytheism (ahl al-shirk). This resembles the saying of Abu Nadra.

Fifth: "Abiding therein, except what your Lord wills," meaning what He wills of a gift that is not cut off, so that "except" (illa) here carries the meaning of "and" (wa), as in the saying of the poet:

Every brother is parted from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads (and the two Farqads).

That is, "and the two Farqads."

Regarding ﴿a gift not cut off﴾ there are two aspects:
One of them: not severed.
The second: not withheld.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 112–113:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

(p-508) The first: "Do not incline toward them," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "Do not draw near to them," said by Sufyan.

The third: "Do not approve of their deeds," said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fourth: "Do not flatter them in speech," which means to agree with them in private and not to denounce them openly.

From the same category is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9], said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

﴿Lest the Fire touch you﴾ admits of two meanings: The first: the punishment of the Fire will touch you because of your inclination toward them.

The second: their wrongdoing will spread to you just as fire spreads to burn what is adjacent to it, and the mention of the Fire in this sense is a metaphor (isti'arah) and a figurative comparison (tashbih). In the first sense, it is a report and a warning (wa'id).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 114–115:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. As for the first end, it is the Fajr prayer by consensus. As for the second end, there are three opinions concerning it:

First: that it refers to the Dhuhr and ʿAṣr prayers. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: the ʿAṣr prayer alone. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: the Maghrib prayer. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And at the approaches of the night﴾. Zulaf is the plural of zulfah, and zulfah means a station (manzilah). So it is as if He said: "and stations of the night", that is, hours of the night. It was said that Muzdalifah was named after this because it is a station (manzil) after ʿArafah. It was also said that it was named so because of the drawing near (izdilaf) of Adam from ʿArafah to Eve, who was there. From this is the verse of al-ʿAjjaj describing a camel:

؎ A swift one, whom weariness and what it endured have folded, the folding of the nights, approach upon approach.

Regarding ﴿and at the approaches of the night﴾ there are two opinions:

One: the late night prayer (ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ and the late prayer. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Hasan, and he related it as a marfūʿ report.

﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾. Concerning these good deeds there are four opinions:

First: the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Masʿud and al-Dahhak.

Second: they are the words "Subhan Allah", "al-Hamdu lillah", "la ilaha illa Allah" and "Allahu Akbar". This was said by Mujahid. ʿAta said: "They are the enduring good deeds (al-Baqiyat al-Salihat)."

Third: that the accepted good deeds remove the forgiven evil deeds.

Fourth: that the reward of acts of obedience removes the punishment for sins.

﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions: One: a repentance for those who repent. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: an explanation for those who take heed. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it."

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Aswad related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, I pursued a woman in one of the outskirts of Madinah, and I got from her everything short of intercourse. I am here, so judge me as you wish."

ʿUmar said to him: "Allah would have concealed you had you concealed yourself."

The Prophet (ﷺ) did not respond to him with anything.

Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) called him and recited it to him. ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it for him specifically or for all people?" He said: "Rather, it is for all people." Abu Musa Tammahan said: this man is Abu al-Yasar al-Ansari. Ibn ʿAbbas said he was ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyyah al-Ansari, and Muqatil said he was ʿAmir ibn Qays al-Ansari.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verses 116–117:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of remainder (uwlu baqiyyah) who would forbid corruption on earth—except a few of those We saved from among them?﴾ In this there are three interpretations. The first: they are people of obedience (uwlu ta'ah).

The second: people of discernment (uwlu tamyiz).

The third: people of caution (uwlu hadhar) before Allah, may He be exalted.

﴿...and those who did wrong pursued what they were given in luxury therein, and they were criminals.﴾ This admits of two meanings. The first: that they pursued, in their wrongdoing, what they were given in luxury therein, from the continuation of His blessings, as a gradual leading-on for them (istidraj).

The second: that they were seized for their wrongdoing regarding what they had been given in luxury from their blessings.

And al-mutraf (the one given luxury) means the one made affluent.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Utrifu fihi" means: look into it (unzuru fihi).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 118–119:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: [one community] upon the religion of Islam alone. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: [one community] of the people of one religion, [namely] the people of misguidance and the people of guidance. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾. Regarding this there are six opinions. The first: they differ in religions, except those among the people of truth upon whom your Lord has mercy. This was said by Mujahid and Ata'.

The second: they differ regarding truth and falsehood, except those among the people of obedience upon whom your Lord has mercy. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they differ in provision, so this one is rich and that one is poor, except those among the people of contentment upon whom your Lord has mercy. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: they differ in misery and happiness, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy with success (tawfiq).

The fifth: they differ in forgiveness and punishment, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy with Paradise.

The sixth: the meaning of "differing" (mukhtalifin) is that some of them succeed (yukhlifu) others, so that whoever comes later is a successor (khalaf) to the one who passed, because each of them was a evil successor to the other, so they fought one another. From this is their saying: "The two new things did not succeed one another (ma ikhtalaf al-jadidan)," meaning this came after that. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And for that He created them﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: He created them for differing. This was said by al-Hasan and Ata'.

The second: He created them for mercy. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: He created them for misery and happiness. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-512) The fourth: He created them for Paradise and Hellfire. This was said by Mansur ibn Abd al-Rahman.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 11, verse 120:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart﴾. That is, We strengthen your heart through it, and your soul finds tranquility in it, because they were tested and they were patient, and they struggled and they prevailed.

﴿And there has come to you in this the truth﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: "in this" refers to this surah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Musa.

The second: "in this" refers to this world (al-dunya). This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The third: "in this" refers to these narratives (al-anba'). This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

In this [word] ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾ there are two interpretations. One: the truth of the narratives and the soundness of the reports; this is the interpretation of those who took the intended meaning to be the surah.

The second: prophethood; this is the interpretation of those who took the intended meaning to be the worldly life (al-dunya).
